995.title: Women in the reform
995.hook: women taught, marched, wrote and went to jail in these movements
995.howItsDone: Sikh histories, gurdwara programs and community events tell the stories of women in the reform movements, and the girls' schools and women's organizations of those years are remembered as part of that work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sant Attar Singh, and your line was schools, not only temples. Did you help a school in some small way? Today, the people the old photographs often leave out of the frame. Day nine hundred ninety-five.

Look closely at a group photograph from the reform years: rows of men in dark turbans, staring straight at the camera. Look at the edges. Behind them, half in shadow, a woman in a white chunni. In some pictures she's not there at all, and yet she cooked the langar the jatha ate before it left, sewed the banners, ran the school, wrote the letters to the newspaper, and sometimes walked in the jatha herself. These last weeks have been full of men's names. Today: women in the reform.
screen: `A PHOTO FULL OF TURBANS.` → `A WOMAN AT THE EDGE.` → `SOMETIMES SHE WALKED TOO.`

segments.voice: First, the classroom. Earlier in this block we met the school for girls at Ferozepur. Bibi Harnam Kaur worked alongside her husband, Bhai Takht Singh, to build it, and women like her taught there, so that girls could read Gurmukhi and the Guru Granth Sahib for themselves. Second, the press. Women wrote too: poems, essays and letters in the Sikh papers of the time, arguing for girls' education and for reform. Third, the march and the jail. In the Ghadar story, Bibi Gulab Kaur is remembered as a woman who went back to India to work for its freedom when her husband turned back, and who was imprisoned for it. In the gurdwara campaigns, women joined the morchas and the jathas, and histories of the Akali movement name women, such as Bibi Kishan Kaur Kaunke, among those who were arrested. That's today's line: she marched too. Fourth, the root. We heard this line with Sundri, and it belongs here too. At Ang 473 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak asks why a woman should be called lesser, when from her kings are born. That line was in the scripture long before any reform movement. Some historians read the women of these years as holding the panth to its own scripture. The records are thinner for them than for the men. Names have been lost, and the sources sometimes mention a woman only as someone's wife or mother. That is part of the story too, and it's why remembering the names we do have matters.

996.title: Reform close
996.hook: schools, presses, peaceful protest and a code: the panth renewed itself
996.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Singh Sabha and gurdwara reform movements through their institutions still standing: schools and colleges, Sikh presses and libraries, the SGPC and the Rehat Maryada, and the gurdwaras where the sakas of those years are told.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bibi, and your line was she marched too. Did you learn one new name? Today we close the whole block on reform and renewal, and look back at the road. Day nine hundred ninety-six.

An old house, handed down. The roof leaks, the wiring is strange, someone has painted over the carvings by the door. You could leave. You could tear it down. Or you could do the slow thing: scrape the paint back, fix the roof, find the original drawings and learn how it was meant to be. Through this whole block of the path, that's how the reformers described their own work. Not building a new house. Restoring the one the Gurus left.
screen: `AN OLD HOUSE, HANDED DOWN.` → `NOT A NEW ONE.` → `RESTORING WHAT THE GURUS LEFT.`

segments.voice: First, the voices calling back. The block opened with Baba Dayal turning people back to the formless One, and Baba Ram Singh and the Namdharis, simple and firm, remembered at Malerkotla and in exile in Burma. Second, the schools and presses. The Singh Sabhas in Amritsar and Lahore, Giani Ditt Singh and Professor Gurmukh Singh, Khalsa College, Mahan Kosh, Macauliffe's volumes, Bhai Vir Singh and his heroine Sundri, suniai, the Chief Khalsa Diwan, Anand Karaj, and the presses that spread it all. Sikhs learned to explain their faith in print, in Punjabi and in English. Third, peaceful protest. Kandh, the outrage over siropa, the SGPC, Tarn Taran and Nankana, the keys, bagh, Panja Sahib and Jaito, until gurdwara gave the shrines back to the sangat. Beside them stood the Ghadar workers far from home, and men like Udham Singh and Bhagat Singh, whose paths Sikhs still weigh. Fourth, the code and the people. Master Tara Singh, the Rehat Maryada, Jail Letters, sung from his cell, Sant Attar Singh's schools, and the women who taught, wrote and marched. Underneath it all is a line from the Japji, at Ang 4 of the Guru Granth Sahib. Guru Nanak says that when hands and feet are muddy, water washes them clean, and when the mind is stained, it is washed by love of the Name. Washing is not a one-time event. You do it again. That's today's line, and the block's: renew.
screen: `VOICES CALLING BACK.` · `SCHOOLS AND PRESSES.` · `PEACEFUL PROTEST.` · `THE CODE AND THE PEOPLE.` · then, large: `RENEW.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of washing. Sit, and let your hands rest in your lap. Bring to mind one practice or habit in your own life that used to be clear and has grown cloudy: a prayer you used to say, a walk you used to take, a promise you used to keep, a way you used to speak to someone. Don't scold yourself. Just look at it, the way you'd look at a smudged window. Breathe in, and see it as it was. Breathe out, and picture wiping the glass clean. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sudhar, reform or improvement: the gurdwara reform movement is called the Gurdwara Sudhar Lehar. Schools, presses, peaceful protest and a shared code helped the panth renew itself. Today's word.

Your line: renew. Today, renew one thing in you: pick up one good habit that has slipped, and do it once, today, as if for the first time. Tomorrow the story leaves Punjab again, for the trenches. Day nine hundred ninety-six.

997.title: The trenches, 1914
997.hook: Sikh soldiers fought in France, Gallipoli and Mesopotamia
997.howItsDone: Some gurdwaras and Sikh community groups, especially in Britain, hold remembrance events for Sikh soldiers of the First World War, and the Ardas said at the close of worship remembers those who gave their lives for others.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the reform years, sudhar: schools, presses, peaceful protest and a code. Your line was renew. What did you renew in yourself? Today a new part of the long story begins, the twentieth century and today. Day nine hundred ninety-seven.

Mud to the knee, rain that won't stop, and a letter being written by the light of a stub of candle. The man writing it is a Sikh soldier in France, a very long way from the wheat fields and the gurdwara of his village. When war broke out in Europe in 1914, soldiers of the Indian Army were sent across the sea, and Sikhs were among them. Some went into the trenches of France and Flanders. Others were sent to Gallipoli, and others to Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and the Euphrates. The last part of the long story opens here, in a trench.
screen: `A LETTER BY CANDLELIGHT.` → `ACROSS THE SEA.` → `FRANCE, GALLIPOLI, MESOPOTAMIA.`

segments.voice: First, the strangeness. These were men who grew up under the Punjab sun, and they were sent into a European winter and a war of trenches and shellfire. The ground, the weather, the food, the language: all of it was foreign. Second, the letters. Soldiers wrote home, or asked a friend who could write to do it for them, and army censors read the letters before they went on. Some censors copied out extracts, and historians have since gathered them into a book. In them men write about the cold, about friends who fell, about the strange country around them, and about wanting news from home. They ask their families to pray for them. Third, what came with them. A Sikh doesn't need a building to pray. The Ardas, the standing prayer that closes Sikh worship, can be said anywhere. In it the panth remembers the Gurus and those who gave everything, and asks for the good of all, sarbat da bhala. A soldier in a trench could stand, fold his hands, and say it in the same words his family used in the village gurdwara. Tradition says regiments kept the Guru Granth Sahib with them where they could, so the sangat traveled too. Fourth, the cost. Not all of them came home. Some are remembered on war memorials far from the rivers they grew up beside, and their families kept their names. That's today's line: far from punjab. A good deal of this century's Sikh story happens far from Punjab, and the prayer goes with it.
screen: `A FOREIGN WINTER, A FOREIGN WAR.` · `LETTERS HOME, READ BY CENSORS.` · `THE ARDAS CAN BE SAID ANYWHERE.` · `NOT ALL OF THEM CAME HOME.` · then, large: `FAR FROM PUNJAB.`

998.title: Turbans, not helmets
998.hook: Sikh soldiers kept their turbans instead of steel helmets
998.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep their hair uncut tie the dastar each morning; Sikh men wear it as the Rehat Maryada asks, and some Sikh women wear one as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the trenches, and your line was far from punjab. Did you thank someone who served? Today we stay at the front, and look at what the soldiers wore on their heads. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

Two things on a table. One is a steel helmet, round and heavy, the kind armies issued in that war against flying metal. The other is a long strip of cloth, folded, waiting to be tied. Every morning in the trenches, a Sikh soldier picked up the cloth. When the helmets came, the soldiers were asked to wear them. The accounts from the war say Sikh soldiers kept their turbans and went into the line without the steel. Why would a man in a place where flying metal could kill him choose cloth over steel? The answer starts with the hair underneath.
screen: `A STEEL HELMET.` → `A STRIP OF CLOTH.` → `THEY KEPT THE CLOTH.`

segments.voice: First, the hair. Kesh, uncut hair, is one of the five articles a Khalsa Sikh keeps, along with the comb, the steel bracelet, the short sword and the cotton undergarment. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, asks Sikhs to keep their hair uncut, as it grew. Second, the turban. The dastar covers and keeps that hair. The code asks Sikh men to wear one, and some Sikh women wear one too. It isn't a hat. A hat comes off at the door. The turban is part of how a Sikh keeps the Guru's form, and it is spoken of as a crown. Third, the helmet. A steel helmet would not sit over a turban, and taking off the turban to fit one would mean setting aside what the code asks a Sikh to wear over uncut hair. So the accounts say the soldiers kept their turbans, and took the danger that came with that. The turban stayed. Fourth, what it says today. A turban can be seen from across a street. It tells everyone who you are before you speak, which is a kind of courage on an ordinary Tuesday, in an office, on a bus, at a school gate. The soldiers wore it into the trenches. Sikhs today tie it before work. That's today's line: the turban stayed.

If you wear a turban, a kara, a cross, a scarf, a ring that means something, feel it now: its weight, where it touches you. If you wear nothing like that, think of one thing about you that people can see and that you'd keep even when it costs you: an accent, a name, a habit of kindness. Breathe in, and own it. Breathe out, and let the worry about other people's eyes loosen. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

999.title: The Second World War
999.hook: Sikhs fought in Italy, Burma and North Africa
999.howItsDone: Some Sikh families keep photographs and medals of relatives who served in the Second World War, and some gurdwaras and community groups mark remembrance days for Sikh soldiers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cloth over steel, and your line was the turban stayed. What did you wear that says who you are? Today the soldiers' sons go to war. Day nine hundred ninety-nine.

Some families keep a tin box on a high shelf, brought down only when a grandchild asks. Inside: a medal on a faded ribbon, a cap badge, a folded paper with a regiment's name on it. In some Sikh families the man those things belonged to is a grandfather or a great-grandfather, and the box has moved house with them, from a village in Punjab to Delhi, or Birmingham, or Toronto. A generation after the trenches, war came again. And Sikhs went again: into the deserts of North Africa, up the mountains of Italy, and through the jungles of Burma.
screen: `A TIN BOX ON A HIGH SHELF.` → `A MEDAL, A BADGE, A REGIMENT.` → `WAR CAME AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the second call. The fathers had come home from France and Mesopotamia, or had not. Now their sons enlisted in the Indian Army for a new war, and Sikhs served in it alongside Hindus, Muslims and others. Second, three landscapes. In North Africa it was sand, heat and thirst. In Italy it was rivers and steep hillsides, taken one ridge at a time. In Burma it was rain, mud and forest so thick you could lose the man in front of you. Same turbans, same Ardas, a different world each time. Third, the measure. At Ang 1105 of the Guru Granth Sahib, a verse of Kabir names the true warrior: the one who fights for the sake of deen, a word some translators render the helpless and others the faith, and who, though cut to pieces, never leaves the field. Some readers hear a battlefield in it. Others hear the fight inside a person, against anger and greed. The verse can hold both. Sikhs have a name for an ideal that joins them, sant-sipahi, the saint-soldier: someone whose bravery is held inside devotion and restraint. Fourth, the generation. The young men in those photographs came home to a country about to be divided, which is where this block of the story is going next. To some grandchildren they were old men at the gurdwara, or in a chair by the window, and only the box on the shelf remembers them young. That's today's line: they served again.

1000.title: A thousand days
1000.hook: day one thousand on the hill: a moment to be glad you came this far
1000.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of chardi kala, rising spirits, as the outlook to keep in good times and hard ones, and the Ardas said at the close of worship ends by asking for chardi kala and the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sant-sipahi, and your line was they served again. Did you ask an older person what they remember? Today the story pauses, because of the number on the bell. Day one thousand.

The hill doesn't hand out trophies. There's no holy day on any calendar for this one, just a count of mornings and evenings when you opened this and listened. But before the story turns toward a very hard year, which it does tomorrow, it's worth stopping on the path, turning around, and looking back down at the first step, far below. So today there's no battle and no reform campaign. There's the place you started, and the place you're standing.
screen: `DAY ONE THOUSAND.` → `STOP ON THE PATH.` → `LOOK BACK DOWN THE HILL.`

segments.voice: First, where you began. Day one on this path was a kitchen in Amritsar that feeds everyone who walks in, for free, and the word was seva, selfless service. Your line that day was one quiet thing for someone. Second, the next step. Day two was Waheguru, the word Sikhs say for God, and the line was simply wow: wonder before the One. Everything since has been built on those two. Gurus and their hymns, martyrs and builders, soldiers and reformers, and a free kitchen that kept feeding strangers all the way through. Third, the spirit for the road. Sikhs have a phrase for the mood they hope to carry through good years and terrible ones: chardi kala. It means rising spirits, an upward-climbing heart. It isn't pretending things are fine. It's staying turned toward the light when they're not. The Ardas, the standing prayer you met three days ago in a trench, closes by asking that through Nanak the Name may bring rising spirits, and that by God's will all may be well. Chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, side by side. Fourth, the next stretch. The story is about to go through the year of Partition, and it won't be easy to hear. Chardi kala is not a way of skipping the hard chapters. It's how Sikhs have walked through them. That's today's line: a thousand days. Not a finish line. A place to stand for a moment, glad, before the path goes on.
screen: `DAY ONE: SEVA, A KITCHEN IN AMRITSAR.` · `DAY TWO: WAHEGURU, WOW.` · `CHARDI KALA: RISING SPIRITS.` · `NOT A WAY AROUND THE HARD PARTS.` · then, large: `A THOUSAND DAYS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes looking back. Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Go back to where you were when you began this path: the room, the season, what was on your mind then. Chardi kala, rising spirits, an upward-climbing heart: a long count of ordinary mornings on the path, from seva and Waheguru to here. Today's word.
Your line: a place to stand, glad. Today, do one quiet thing for someone, the way day one asked, and notice that you still can. Day one thousand.

1001.title: Rawalpindi, March 1947
1001.hook: months before Partition, Sikh villages near Rawalpindi were attacked, and women took their own lives rather than be taken
1001.howItsDone: Sikh families from the Rawalpindi villages and their descendants remember the women of March 1947 as martyrs, and the story is retold in the community and in histories of Partition.

segments.voice: Yesterday you stood on the path and looked back, and your line was a place to stand, glad. Today the story goes on, into a hard chapter. Take it slowly. Day one thousand one.

A well in the courtyard of a village gurdwara, in the hills near Rawalpindi, in what is now Pakistan. In March of 1947, months before the border was drawn, armed mobs attacked Sikh and Hindu villages across that district. Houses burned. People were killed. In the village of Thoa Khalsa, survivors later told a historian, a large group of the village's women went into the well rather than be taken by the attackers. This lesson will not linger on how. It stays with the women, and with how they are remembered.
screen: `A WELL IN A VILLAGE COURTYARD.` → `MARCH, MONTHS BEFORE THE BORDER.` → `THE WOMEN OF THOA KHALSA.`

segments.voice: First, before the border. Partition is often told as a story that began when the line was drawn. Rawalpindi is a reminder that the killing started earlier, while the politicians were still talking. Second, the listener. The historian Urvashi Butalia sat with Partition survivors and recorded their memories, and she wrote about Thoa Khalsa. The families who survived remember those women as martyrs, shaheed, who chose death over capture and dishonor. Each year, she wrote, the story was retold to the community. Third, a harder question, asked gently. Butalia also asked how much choice the women had, when fathers and brothers and the fear of capture stood around them. She didn't throw out the families' memory. She held it next to the question, and let both stand. That's a kind of respect too: refusing to make anyone's death simpler than it was. Fourth, an older grief. Tradition says Guru Nanak himself saw an invading army sweep across Punjab, and in hymns kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, at Ang 417, he mourned for women whose braided hair, once parted with vermilion, was shorn, and whose finery was taken. The Guru's own words didn't look away from what war does to women. So this week, which ran from women marching in the reform years, through the trenches, the turbans, a second war and a thousand days, ends here at a well. Not with an explanation. With a name, Thoa Khalsa, and a decision to remember. That's today's line: hold them gently.
screen: `THE KILLING STARTED BEFORE THE BORDER.` · `THE FAMILIES REMEMBER MARTYRS.` · `HOW MUCH CHOICE DID THEY HAVE?` · `GURU NANAK MOURNED TOO: ANG 417.` · then, large: `HOLD THEM GENTLY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of silence, gently. If this story is close to your own family's, go easy with yourself, and stop whenever you need to. Sit, and let the hands rest. You don't need to picture anything. Just hold the women of those villages in mind, without faces, without details, the way you'd hold someone's hand at a funeral. Breathe in, and let them be remembered. Breathe out, and let the silence do the rest. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Rawalpindi. The district in the hills where, months before Partition, Sikh and Hindu villages were attacked, and the women of Thoa Khalsa died rather than be taken. Today's word.
Your line: hold them gently. Today, if someone tells you a hard story from their family, hold it gently: listen to the end, and don't hurry them. Day one thousand one.

fork.setup: you're a historian. the survivors tell you the women of the village chose martyrdom. what do you do?
options: set their memory aside as legend.
write down only their version, with no questions.
honor their memory, and also ask how much choice the women had.
fork.reveal: Urvashi Butalia did both: she recorded the families' memory of martyrdom and gently asked how free the women's choice was, letting both stand.
